clinician.trajectory_summary: A 20-year-old man with a history of right tibial osteosarcoma (treated with supracondylar amputation at age 17) and recent diagnosis of brain and lung metastases presented with 2-week progressive vision loss in the right eye (hand movements vision OD, 20/20 OS). Ophthalmic examination revealed a large, posterior pole, pink, nodular subretinal mass with associated fluid. Multimodal imaging characterized a calcified choroidal mass: B-scan ultrasonography (E002) demonstrated a heterogeneous subretinal mass with medium/high internal reflectivity, areas of localized increased and decreased reflectivity (suggesting necrosis/air), and height-to-base ratio of 1-1.2; MRI (E004) showed T1-isointense and T2-hypointense signal consistent with calcification; CT (E003) confirmed a heterogeneous, hyperdense, well-defined uveal mass with contrast enhancement. During follow-up, the ocular lesion demonstrated radiographic response to systemic treatment with decreased volume on repeat CT and MRI (E006). The diagnosis was established based on the characteristic imaging features of a calcified choroidal mass in the context of widespread metastatic osteosarcoma, without requirement for histopathological confirmation given the clinical context.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Imaging characteristics inconsistent with melanoma (T2 hypointensity suggests calcification rather than melanin's T1 hyperintensity/T2 hypointensity pattern, and B-scan features suggest calcified rather than solid melanotic mass)
Hemangioma typically shows high internal reflectivity on B-scan and lacks the heterogeneous calcification patterns and necrosis seen here
Age 20 is atypical for retinoblastoma, and patient has known metastatic osteosarcoma providing alternative etiology
